{{Short description|Axiom in set theory}}
In [[mathematics]], the '''axiom of finite choice''' is a weak version of the [[axiom of choice]] which asserts that if <math>(S_\alpha)_{\alpha \in A}</math> is a family of [[empty set|non-empty]] ''[[finite set]]s'', then
:<math>\prod_{\alpha \in A} S_\alpha \neq \emptyset </math> ([[Cartesian product#Infinite products|set-theoretic product]]).<ref name="herrlich" />{{rp|14}}
If every set can be [[total order|linearly ordered]], the axiom of finite choice follows.<ref name="herrlich" />{{rp|17}}

== Applications ==
An important application is that when <math>(\Omega, 2^\Omega, \nu)</math> is a [[measure space]] where <math>\nu</math> is the [[counting measure]] and <math>f: \Omega \to \mathbb R</math> is a [[function (mathematics)|function]] such that
:<math>\int_\Omega |f| d \nu < \infty</math>,
then <math>f(\omega) \neq 0</math> for at most [[countable|countably many]] <math>\omega \in \Omega</math>.
